case_analysis.thread_summary: The thread discusses Bluetooth SIG qualification strategy for a wearable BLE product using an SoC controller design combined with an existing host stack under the new QPRDv3 qualification system. The main issue is that the selected Host and Controller combinations fail the new inter-layer consistency checks introduced after the July 2024 Qualification Workspace migration. The consultant explains multiple registration paths, including legacy-style combination registration without a Design Number (DN), versus creating a DN-bearing design through a different architecture strategy. The discussion evolves toward a practical workaround where the module is qualified as a Core Controller design with RF PHY testing, allowing downstream OEM customers to reuse the resulting DN in their own product registrations.
case_analysis.key_technical_discussion: The primary technical issue is inter-layer dependency inconsistency between GAP and LL ICS selections when combining the selected Host and Controller designs. The detected inconsistencies involve Periodic Advertising, Synchronization, and Periodic Advertising Sync Transfer capabilities where the GAP layer claims support for features not supported by the LL layer. The consultant explains that correcting ICS mismatches would trigger additional protocol-layer testing obligations under QPRDv3 because modifying ICS selections changes qualification scope. The thread also clarifies how the new Qualification Workspace handles Design Numbers, including cases where registrations using unmodified combined designs may display 'Details' or issue Q30-series DNs. The final proposed solution avoids modifying incompatible Host/Controller combinations by qualifying only the SoC-based controller module with RF PHY testing and allowing downstream products to include that DN without triggering the problematic consistency checks.
case_analysis.key_decision_logic: The consultant's reasoning is driven by minimizing qualification risk and avoiding unnecessary protocol testing caused by ICS modifications. Because the Host and Controller designs contain incompatible inter-layer dependencies, directly correcting the ICS would likely require extensive GAP and protocol-stack testing that is difficult without deep stack vendor access. Instead of forcing protocol-layer remediation, the consultant recommends restructuring the qualification approach so the module is qualified independently as a Core Controller design with only required RF PHY testing. This preserves the ability for OEM customers to reference a valid DN while avoiding costly and operationally risky Host/GAP remediation work.
case_analysis.risk_if_done_wrong: If the incompatible Host and Controller designs were modified directly to satisfy consistency checks, additional mandatory protocol-layer testing could be triggered under QPRDv3. The consultant warns that this could require debugger integration into upper protocol layers, repeated failure analysis, software modification, recompilation, and retesting, which may be impractical without support from the original stack vendor. Selecting the wrong qualification path could also result in registrations without usable DN references for downstream OEM customers, creating qualification complications for future products. Incorrect handling of RF PHY scope could additionally increase unnecessary testing cost from a 1M-only PHY test plan to broader PHY coverage.
case_analysis.consulting_takeaway: Under QPRDv3, consultants must evaluate inter-layer dependency consistency before recommending reuse of existing Host and Controller designs. When ICS inconsistencies exist, modifying the ICS can unintentionally expand qualification scope and trigger significant additional testing obligations. In many cases, restructuring the qualification architecture to isolate reusable compliant designs is more practical than attempting to repair incompatible inherited stacks. For OEM-oriented products, preserving issuance of a reusable DN is often strategically more important than minimizing initial registration complexity.
